days.title: Reactions That Produce & Consume ATP
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Identify reactions that produce ATP.
  • Identify reactions that consume ATP.
  • Explain the ATP-ADP cycle.
  • Relate ATP turnover to cell activity.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • ATP-ADP cycle — continuous regeneration of ATP.
  • Substrate-level phosphorylation — direct ATP formation.
  • Oxidative phosphorylation — ATP via ETC + chemiosmosis.
  • Photophosphorylation — ATP via light-driven ETC.

📚 Lesson Content

A. ATP-Producing Reactions

  • Glycolysis (substrate-level)
  • Krebs cycle (substrate-level)
  • Oxidative phosphorylation (ETC + chemiosmosis) — the biggest producer
  • Light reactions (photophosphorylation)

B. ATP-Consuming Reactions

  • Calvin cycle (uses ATP + NADPH)
  • Active transport (Na⁺/K⁺ pump)
  • Muscle contraction
  • Protein synthesis
  • Cell division

C. ATP Turnover

A typical cell uses and regenerates ~10 million ATP molecules per second. ATP is not stored — it is generated on demand.

scenarios.text: Glucose → pyruvate with 2 ATP produced.
CO₂ → glucose in the Calvin cycle.
Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves ions against the gradient.
Electrons flow through the ETC.
Muscle fibers contract.
Ribosomes assemble proteins.

questions.text: Which process produces the most ATP?
Which of the following consumes ATP?

takeaways: ATP is produced in glycolysis, Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and photophosphorylation.
ATP is consumed in the Calvin cycle, active transport, muscle contraction, and biosynthesis.
ATP turnover is rapid — ATP is generated on demand.
The ATP-ADP cycle maintains cellular energy balance.

days.title: ATP Accounting in Respiration
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compute ATP yield per stage of respiration.
  • Explain why the total is ~36–38 ATP, not 40.
  • Account for ATP used in transport.
  • Interpret ATP yield tables.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • ATP yield — total ATP produced per glucose.
  • NADH — carries 2.5 ATP each (in ETC).
  • FADH₂ — carries 1.5 ATP each.
  • Shuttle cost — 2 ATP used to move NADH into mitochondria.

📚 Lesson Content

ATP Yield Table (per glucose)

StageATPNADHFADH₂
Glycolysis220
Pyruvate oxidation020
Krebs cycle262
Subtotal4102

ETC ATP Conversion

  • 10 NADH × 2.5 ATP = 25 ATP
  • 2 FADH₂ × 1.5 ATP = 3 ATP
  • Substrate-level = 4 ATP
  • Total = 32 ATP (modern estimate)
  • Older textbooks say 36–38 (using 3 ATP/NADH)

days.title: ATP Accounting in Photosynthesis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Compute ATP and NADPH used in the Calvin cycle.
  • Explain the ATP/NADPH ratio needed.
  • Compare ATP usage in photosynthesis vs respiration.
  • Summarize photosynthesis energetics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Calvin cycle cost — 18 ATP + 12 NADPH per glucose.
  • Ratio — 3 ATP : 2 NADPH per CO₂ fixed.
  • Photophosphorylation — ATP production in light reactions.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Calvin Cycle Cost (per glucose)

  • 6 CO₂ fixed
  • 18 ATP used
  • 12 NADPH used
  • Produces 1 glucose

B. Per CO₂ Fixed

  • 3 ATP
  • 2 NADPH

C. ATP/NADPH Ratio

The light reactions must produce ATP and NADPH in a 3:2 ratio to match the Calvin cycle's needs.

days.title: Oxygen's Role & Anaerobic Pathways
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain the role of oxygen in respiration.
  • Describe electron flow without oxygen.
  • Explain fermentation pathways.
  • Compare anaerobic vs aerobic energetics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • O₂ — final electron acceptor in ETC.
  • Anaerobic respiration — ETC without O₂ (using other acceptors).
  • Fermentation — regenerates NAD⁺ without ETC.
  • Lactate / ethanol — fermentation end products.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Oxygen's Role

  • Accepts electrons at the end of ETC
  • Combines with H⁺ → H₂O
  • Keeps ETC running
  • Without O₂: ETC halts → NADH accumulates

B. Anaerobic Pathways

PathwayEnd ProductWhere
Lactic acid fermentationLactateMuscle cells, bacteria (yogurt)
Alcoholic fermentationEthanol + CO₂Yeast, some bacteria

C. Why Fermentation Matters

Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue producing 2 ATP per glucose — enough for short bursts of activity.
